lesson.menu_title: If I Have Time This Weekend
lesson.menu_desc: The same if-sentence is a firm promise in Hamburg and a polite maybe in Sao Paulo. Tonight, the first conditional and the small words that decide how much you are promising
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- If I Have Time This Weekend
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 12 -- If I Have Time This Weekend
lesson.grammar_point: first conditional with unless, in case and as long as

listenings.text: My name is Anke. I grew up near Hamburg, and I have lived in Lisbon for six years. The first thing that confused me here was the weekend. In Germany, if you invite me to a barbecue on Saturday, I will write it down, and I will come. If it rains, we will have a fallback, usually somebody's garage. We almost never call things off at the last minute. Here, people say, if I have time, I will come, and I believed them. For months I waited for friends who were never going to arrive. Now I understand that a plan like that is tentative. It is not a promise. So I have changed too. I pencil things in, and I only commit to something when I really know. And if a Portuguese friend says maybe, I do not wait by the door any more. I bring a book.

I am Liam, and I come from a small town in Queensland. People from overseas think Australians never plan anything, and they are half right. On a Friday my friends and I will say, let's go fishing tomorrow, and then we play it by ear. If the weather looks iffy in the morning, we just stay home. Everything hinges on the sky. Last summer there was a massive downpour on the day of my brother's birthday, and half the guests took a rain check. Nobody was offended. That is the part visitors find strange. If you back out of a plan here, you say sorry, next time, and that is the end of it. My wife is German, and she still cannot believe it. She says, if you promise something, you do it. And to be honest, she has a point.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: A second plan that you use if the first one fails
To say no for now, but suggest another time
Not definite yet, and it can still change
To decide not to do something you agreed to do
To depend completely on one thing

vocab.text: Look at how many of these words describe a plan that is NOT fixed yet: tentative, iffy, to pencil something in, to play it by ear. English has a whole vocabulary for plans that might change, and that is exactly the territory of the first conditional.

reading.rtitle: If I Have Time, I Will Come
paras: Every culture has a sentence that sounds like a plan and works like a door left open. In Brazil it is often if I have time, I will come. Everybody at the table understands that the plan is tentative, and nobody is hurt when the person does not arrive.

Take the same sentence to Hamburg and it becomes something else. A German listener hears a condition, and a condition is close to a contract: if the condition is true, you will come. If it rains, there will be a fallback. People do call things off, but rarely at the last minute, and almost never without saying so.

Australians sit somewhere in between. Plans hinge on the weather, the waves and the mood, and everybody is happy to play it by ear. If the forecast looks iffy, nobody commits to anything until the morning, and taking a rain check is not rude at all.

Grammatically, the three cultures use exactly the same structure: if plus the present, then will. What changes is how much of a promise the listener hears. So at this level the useful skill is not the form but the words around it. Unless makes the exception clear. As long as sets a firm condition. In case is not a condition at all: it is a precaution. Choose well, and a German friend will know exactly when to expect you.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: How the weather decides weekend plans in three countries
The same if-sentence carries a different level of promise in different cultures, and English has small words to make it precise
Why Germans are more reliable than Brazilians

items: In Brazil, if I have time, I will come usually means a firm yes.
The text says everybody understands the plan is tentative — a door left open, not a promise.
A German listener hears the if-sentence as something close to a contract.
If the condition is true, you will come, and if it rains there will be a fallback.
The text says Australians are rude because they take rain checks.
It says the opposite: taking a rain check is not rude at all there.
The three cultures use different grammar for the same idea.
They use exactly the same structure. What changes is how much of a promise the listener hears.
In case describes a precaution, not a condition.
You do the thing anyway, whether or not the event happens.

items.situation: A German friend invites you to a barbecue on Saturday. Give her a clear answer with one condition and a time.
tips: If it does not rain, I will be there at one.
A condition plus a time sounds like a promise in Germany.

items.situation: Say yes to a hike, with one exception only.
tips: I will come, unless my sister visits that day.
Unless means if not. Never put not after it.

items.situation: Say what you will take with you, as a precaution.
tips: I will take a jacket in case it gets cold.
In case: you take it anyway, even if the cold never comes.

items.situation: Say no to dinner tonight, politely, and leave the door open for another day.
tips: Can I take a rain check? I am free next weekend.
A rain check says no now, yes later.

items.situation: An Australian friend says: let's play it by ear. Find out what the plan really depends on.
tips: Sure. What does it hinge on, the weather?
Hinge on means depend completely on one thing.

items.situation: Tell a friend your plan is not fixed yet, and when you will confirm.
tips: It is only tentative. Can we pencil it in and confirm on Friday?
Tentative and pencil in both say: this can still change.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
key: The basic form: If it rains, we will call it off. Present after if, will in the other half.
Never will after if: If it rains · never if it will rain.
The exception: I will come unless it rains. Unless already means if not.
The firm condition: I will come as long as we leave before eight.
The precaution: I will take a jacket in case it gets cold. It is not a condition.
Certain versus possible: When I get home, I will call you. If I have time, I will call you.
The polite no: Can I take a rain check? I am free next weekend.
And the one that is not grammar: in some cultures if I have time is a maybe, in others it is a promise. Say which one you mean.
